progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: See the Scope paragraph. Not assumed: cell cycle (as a term), checkpoint, p53, apoptosis, proto-oncogene, oncogene, tumour suppressor gene, melanocyte, tumour (b06 used the word with a short meaning; re-glossed), benign, malignant, basement membrane, metastasis, secondary tumour, lymph vessel (Year 11 knowledge is thin; glossed on screen).
progression.startsWith: Every day, your body makes huge numbers of new cells by mitosis, and each time DNA is copied, a few changes can slip through. So most of us carry cells with changed DNA. Yet most of those cells never become cancer. Why not? And when one does, how does it spread? That's today's question: how does cancer begin and spread?
progression.stopsAfter: saying that a cancer cell still divides by mitosis and that the main failure is control of when it divides; describing the cell cycle as grow, copy DNA, get ready, divide, with checkpoints that check it is safe to go on (the one before DNA copying asks about cell size, a signal to divide and DNA damage; the spindle checkpoint recalled); explaining how p53 responds to DNA damage by stopping the cycle for repair or triggering apoptosis, that many mutations don't affect the genes that control division, and why most changed cells therefore never become cancer; explaining that cancer usually needs several mutations in one cell line, each giving its cells a small advantage, so it usually takes years and becomes more common with age; explaining proto-oncogenes (normal accelerators) mutated into oncogenes that signal division with no outside signal, with one mutated copy enough; explaining tumour suppressor genes (brakes: stop division, repair DNA, trigger apoptosis) that usually need both copies lost, and why an inherited faulty copy raises risk without making cancer certain; explaining UV as a named environmental risk for melanoma (DNA damage in melanocytes, an accelerator such as BRAF stuck on, brakes lost, a tumour); distinguishing benign (stays where it started) from malignant (breaks through the basement membrane and invades); describing metastasis as detach, enter a lymph or blood vessel, survive, leave and grow a secondary tumour, usually first in a nearby lymph node for melanoma; explaining why spread causes most cancer deaths and why early removal matters; applying the gene ideas and invasion to two unseen cases.
progression.nextLesson: how common is a disease, and how do we measure it: incidence, prevalence and mortality (bio-m8-b10).

teaching.task: Every day your body makes huge numbers of new cells, and copying DNA lets a few changes slip through, yet most changed cells never become cancer. How does cancer begin, and how does it spread?
teaching.causalExplanation: Start with what you know. Before mitosis, a cell copies its DNA. Mitosis separates the chromosome copies into two nuclei. A cancer cell still divides by mitosis. The main problem isn't how it divides, but when. Healthy cells divide when the body needs them, like when a graze heals. A cancer cell keeps dividing when it should stop. A cell's life runs in a loop called the cell cycle. It grows, copies its DNA, gets ready, then divides. Along the loop sit checkpoints, stops where the cell checks that it's safe to go on. You've met one: before the copies separate, the cell waits until every chromosome is attached to fibres from both poles. Another comes before the DNA is copied. It asks: is the cell big enough, is there a signal to divide, and is the DNA undamaged? At that checkpoint, a protein called p53 responds to DNA damage. It stops the cycle, so repair enzymes can fix the damage. If the damage is too great, p53 triggers apoptosis: the cell destroys itself in a controlled way. And many mutations that do slip through don't affect the genes that control division. That's the first answer. Cancer usually needs several changes that defeat those controls.
teaching.conversationalApproach: Every day, your body makes huge numbers of new cells by mitosis, and each time DNA is copied, a few changes can slip through. Start with what you know. A cell's life runs in a loop called the cell cycle. At that checkpoint, a protein called p53 responds to DNA damage. Those changes usually build up in the same line of cells. Which genes? Two kinds control division. The other kind are tumour suppressor genes, the brakes. Now a real case. Compare that with a benign mole. Spreading to a new site is called metastasis, and it takes several steps. That's why metastasis causes most cancer deaths. Two exam questions. Cell A. Second. Losing p53 weakens a key DNA-damage checkpoint. So for any cancer question, follow the chain: mutations build up, a control breaks, an accelerator stuck on or a brake lost, then division without stopping, a tumour, and, if it's malignant, invasion and spread.
teaching.openingDecision: Every day, your body makes huge numbers of new cells by mitosis, and each time DNA is copied, a few changes can slip through. So most of us carry cells with changed DNA. Yet most of those cells never become cancer. Why not? And when one does, how does it spread? That's today's question: how does cancer begin and spread?
teaching.understandingCheck: Two exam questions. First. Cell A has an activating mutation that keeps one copy of a proto-oncogene switched on. Cell B has a mutation that stops one copy of a tumour suppressor gene working, and one normal copy is enough for that gene's job. Every other copy is normal. Predict which cell is more likely to divide without a growth signal, and explain your prediction. Pause here to answer. Second. Some types of human papillomavirus, or HPV, infect cells lining the cervix. One viral protein, called E6, causes the cell to destroy its p53. Explain how this infection can increase the risk of cancer. Then explain why a growth that hasn't crossed the basement membrane is unlikely to have spread. Pause here to answer.
teaching.curriculumScope: B8-IQ2-01 (p 57): "investigate the causes and effects of non-infectious diseases in humans, including but not limited to:" with the listed example "cancer". Causes: scenes 3 to 8 (control genes, mutation build-up, UV). Effects: scenes 8 to 11 (tumour, invasion, metastasis, why spread kills). Inquiry question: "Do non-infectious diseases cause more deaths than infectious diseases?" (not answered here; b10 and g01 use death data).

design.visualSystem: One coded cause chain owns the bottom fifth from scene 5 to scene 11: five linked boxes, "mutations build up" → "control lost" → "divides without stopping" → "tumour" → "invades and spreads", each lighting on its cue with a small thumbnail; the decision rule replays it. Upper area: one painted plate or matched set at a time, with callouts. The cycle ring (coded: a loop with four stations and three gate marks) sits at the upper left from scene 3 to scene 7, each station holding a small cd- plate thumbnail. Chromosomes are seen only where the cd- plates paint them; DNA damage is shown as small coded amber sparks on the nucleus envelope of cd-interphase-v1.png, never as bars or strands drawn over the cell. No people, hands or faces at any point. At most three bright text items; earlier labels dim to grey.
